recent_posts.title: How computers evolved from vacuum tubes to integrated circuits 1945 to 1977
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive historical overview tracing computer evolution from 1945-1977, covering the transition from vacuum tube mainframes to transistorized systems and early integrated circuits. The content explains how computers progressed from room-sized machines like ENIAC to personal computers, detailing the technological shifts from vacuum tubes to transistors to packaged ICs. It examines IBM's mainframe dominance with the System 360, the development of CPUs like the Intel 4004 and MOS 6502, and why market leaders failed to adapt between technological ages. The video uses 3D models of 60+ devices and Lego brick analogies to visualize computational power increases.

recent_posts.title: How does a Laser Computer Mouse Work? #mouse #howitworks #laser
recent_posts.summary: Computer mice use an infrared LED and low-resolution camera to track movement by capturing thousands of images per second of the surface texture below. The LED shines light at a shallow angle to highlight surface peaks and troughs, similar to sunset lighting on mountains. The camera compares consecutive images to calculate X and Y movements. This explains why mice don't work well on glass—its smooth, transparent surface lacks the texture needed for proper image differentiation.

recent_posts.title: How do Scroll Wheels Work? #mouse #howitworks
recent_posts.summary: A computer mouse scroll wheel uses an optical rotary encoder with 48 evenly spaced slots, an infrared LED, and two light sensors. As the wheel rotates, sensors detect 48 light pulses per revolution. Two adjacent sensors determine rotation direction by detecting which sees light first. The clicking sensation comes from ridges on the wheel and a spring-loaded ball pressing against them.

recent_posts.title: How do Mechanical Keyboards Work? #keyboard #pcbuild
recent_posts.summary: Mechanical keyboards produce their distinctive clicking sound through a precise mechanism inside each key. When pressed, a stem and slider compress a spring, causing a metal contact leaf to snap forward and strike another contact, creating the click. This contact closure allows electricity to flow, registering the keystroke. When released, the spring pushes the slider back up, separating the contacts and resetting the key.

recent_posts.title: How do Power Supplies Work? #pcbuild #powersupply #gamingpc
recent_posts.summary: Power supplies convert 120V AC electricity into 12V, 5V, and 3.3V DC voltages needed by computer components. The conversion process uses high-power switching transistors and transformers regulated by a control PCB, with opto-isolators managing communication between the high-voltage AC and low-voltage DC sides of the unit.

recent_posts.title: How do CPU Water Coolers Work? #pcbuild #watercooling #computerhardware
recent_posts.summary: Explains the mechanics of liquid CPU cooling systems. A water cooler uses a brushless motor with a magnetic rotor to drive an impeller that circulates cooling liquid. The liquid absorbs heat from the CPU, transfers it to radiator fins where fans dissipate it, then returns in a closed loop to repeat the process.

recent_posts.title: How EUV lithography machines create nanoscale microchips
recent_posts.summary: EUV lithography machines use extreme ultraviolet light to pattern nanoscale transistors on silicon wafers, enabling the mass production of modern microchips. The process involves shooting laser pulses at tin droplets to generate 13-nanometer EUV light, which passes through precision mirrors to copy photomask patterns onto wafers with atomic-level accuracy. These machines can pattern billions of transistors measuring just 10 nanometers across, making possible the CPUs, GPUs, and memory chips found in all modern electronics.

recent_posts.title: How do Transistors Work?  How are Transistors Assembled Inside a CPU?
recent_posts.summary: Transistors function as electronic switches that can be combined to create logic gates, which form the building blocks of CPUs. N-type transistors conduct when voltage is applied to their gate, while P-type transistors work in reverse. By connecting these transistors in different configurations, engineers create standard cells like inverters, NAND gates, and AND gates. These standard cells are then assembled into larger functional units called macrocells, which perform complex operations like addition and multiplication. Modern CPUs contain billions of these transistors organized across multiple metal layers, all working together in picoseconds to execute computational tasks.
